terms.grammar: adjective; mīrum est with an accusative and infinitive, quod, or an indirect question
evidence: Ter. Haut. 1: Nē cui sit vestrum mīrum, cūr partēs senī …
Traupman 61: Mīrum est, that’s strange; Traupman 353, 386
terms.comment: What makes one wonder, for good or ill: mīrum est, that’s strange; mīrum in modum, strangely, amazingly; mīrum nī, “I’d be surprised if not”, so “surely”. It is also “wonderful” (see wonderful), and nec mīrum is “no wonder” (see be surprised).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.361 (Lewis & Short): īnsolita mihi loquācitās
terms.comment: Strange because not usual: of a thing, uncommon; of a person, unused to something (īnsolitus ad labōrem, Caes. BC 3.85, Lewis & Short).
Besides “new”, of what is novel and so unusual or strange: novum et mōribus veterum īnsolitum, a strange thing, unknown to the ways of the ancients (Tac. A. 12.37, Lewis & Short; see new).

phrases.latin: Nē cui sit vestrum mīrum, cūr partēs senī poēta dederit quae sunt adolēscentium, id prīmum dīcam
phrases.english: In case any of you thinks it strange that the poet has given an old man a young man’s part, I’ll explain that first
He must be at home (it would be strange if he weren’t).

phrases.latin: Mīrum est, nam valētūdine bonā ūteris.
phrases.english: That’s strange, since you’re in good health.

sources: Lewis & Short: mirus · Lewis & Short: insolitus · Lewis & Short: novus
